nameStory: The name 'firewheel' perfectly captures this flower's blazing appearance - picture a spinning wheel of fire with red petals radiating out from a dark center like glowing spokes. The alternative name 'Indian blanket' comes from the resemblance to the rich red, orange, and yellow patterns found in traditional Native American textiles and blankets.
description: Firewheel is a cheerful wildflower that looks like a daisy wearing sunset colors. The blooms feature bright red petals tipped with yellow, surrounding a deep reddish-brown center that's actually made up of dozens of tiny flowers packed together. These compact plants typically grow 1-2 feet tall with fuzzy, grayish-green leaves and sturdy stems that can handle tough conditions.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive daisy-like blooms with red petals that fade to bright yellow at the tips, surrounding a dark red-brown center that feels slightly bumpy to the touch when mature

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, fuzzy leaves that feel like flannel and are grayish-green in color, with simple oval to lance shapes that alternate up the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, bushy plants that spread outward and typically stay under 2 feet tall, with multiple branching stems that feel sturdy but not woody

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Fluffy, dandelion-like seed heads that form after flowers fade, with seeds that have feathery white plumes for wind dispersal

habitat: In New England, firewheel is most commonly found in disturbed areas, roadsides, and waste places rather than natural habitats, as it's actually native to the central and southern United States. It thrives in poor, sandy or gravelly soils with good drainage and full sun exposure, often appearing in areas where other plants struggle.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fuzzy rosettes of grayish leaves close to the ground. In warmer locations, early flowers may begin appearing by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with the most abundant and vibrant flowers. This is when the red and yellow 'firewheel' display is at its most spectacular.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue blooming into early fall, followed by the formation of fluffy white seed heads that disperse on autumn breezes.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely, surviving only as seeds that will germinate the following spring when conditions warm up.

funFact: Each 'flower' is actually a botanical illusion - what looks like a single bloom is really 50-100 tiny individual flowers working together, with the colorful 'petals' being sterile ray flowers whose only job is to attract pollinators to the fertile disc flowers in the center.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other red-orange daisy-family flowers, but firewheel's distinctive yellow petal tips and grayish fuzzy foliage set it apart. Remember: 'Fire fades to gold' - the red petals always fade to yellow at the tips, unlike solid-colored relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Though beautiful and popular in wildflower seed mixes, firewheel is actually not native to New England - it's a southwestern species that has naturalized here. Many garden centers sell it as a 'wildflower,' but true New England natives would be more ecologically beneficial choices for local pollinators.
compareHints: Firewheel is the only Gaillardia species commonly found in New England, making it easy to distinguish within its genus. Among the broader sunflower family, it's unique for its red-and-yellow color combination and fuzzy gray foliage - most similar species are either solid yellow (like black-eyed Susan) or have green leaves rather than the distinctive grayish, flannel-textured foliage of firewheel.
